THOUGHT: This 79-year-old male presents with chronic progressive dyspnea on exertion and a persistent productive cough—classic respiratory symptoms. His 25-year history of heavy smoking is a major risk factor for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The absence of systemic symptoms (no fever, weight loss, night sweats, or hemoptysis) makes malignancy, active infection, or granulomatous disease less likely at initial assessment. Physical exam findings—including decreased breath sounds, wheezes, basilar crackles, increased resonance to percussion (suggesting air trapping), and normal tactile fremitus—are consistent with emphysematous and chronic bronchitic components of COPD. Spirometry shows a significantly reduced FEV1 (48% predicted), preserved FVC (85%), and an FEV1/FVC ratio of 56% (<70%), confirming persistent airflow obstruction. Chest radiography demonstrates pulmonary hyperinflation and flattened diaphragms—radiographic hallmarks of emphysema. While the crackles may raise concern for heart failure or interstitial lung disease, the absence of orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, elevated JVP, peripheral edema, or cardiac enlargement on imaging (not reported but implied by context), along with the dominant obstructive spirometry pattern and smoking history, strongly favors COPD over heart failure or restrictive lung disease. Asthma is unlikely given late onset, lack of reversibility testing (but chronicity and fixed obstruction on spirometry suggest non-reversible disease), and absence of atopy or episodic wheeze.

DIAGNOSIS: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), predominantly emphysema phenotype, GOLD Stage III (Severe).
